argument: In Sources of the Self and The Ethics of Authenticity, Charles Taylor traces a genealogy of the modern self, showing how Western assumptions about morality and identity shifted from being grounded in one's roles within a cosmic order (ancient Athens), to an inward turn toward God's equally-offered love (Augustine), to disengaged scientific observation of the self (Descartes), to a self that can be deliberately reorganized (Locke) and is grounded in feeling (Hume), to a natural inner self that society corrupts and authenticity must uncover and express (Rousseau and Romanticism). Taylor argues all three resulting strands — religious, instrumental-reason, and Romantic-authenticity — remain necessary and coexist today, and that real authenticity requires acknowledging the shared 'horizons of significance' that ground our choices rather than treating personal preference as a self-generated, self-justifying source of value.
keyIdeas: A genealogy of the modern self traces the changing assumptions people have made at different points in Western history about what a self is and how it relates to morality, to explain why modern people focus so heavily on authenticity.

Ancient Athenians primarily understood the self in terms of roles within families, civic groups, and a cosmic order upheld by the gods, not as a private inner 'true self' to be discovered — a stark contrast with the modern conception.

Descartes' mind-body dualism produced 'disengaged reason': the idea that the self could be studied the way science studies the external world, observed from a neutral, detached 'view from nowhere' rather than known through lived, embedded experience.

Rousseau argued that society corrupts people and that beneath social conditioning lies a truer, more natural self that must be individually discovered, protected, and expressed — a key origin point of the modern hyper-focus on authenticity.

Taylor calls the shared background of narratives, traditions, and values against which meaningful choices are actually made 'horizons of significance'; treating 'good' as simply meaning 'I prefer it' is circular and denies these horizons are actually grounding the choice, whether or not the person realizes it.

terms.def: Taylor's method of tracing the changing historical assumptions about what a self is and how it relates to morality, used in Sources of the Self to explain the modern focus on authenticity.
Taylor's term for the Cartesian view of the self as an object to be observed and assessed from a neutral, detached 'view from nowhere,' rather than known through lived, embedded experience.
John Locke's idea that people are born blank slates without pre-existing knowledge, implying the self can, in principle, be deliberately reorganized into a different kind of person.
Taylor's term for the shared background of narratives, traditions, and values against which meaningful choices are actually made, even when they feel like pure personal preference.

Taylor's term for the modern responsibility placed on individuals to take an unbiased inventory of themselves, decide what kind of person to be, and act on it, with far less of a handbook than people had in earlier eras.
Taylor's requirement that a person be able to say why one choice is better than another; without it, one doesn't actually know the values driving one's own choices.
